title: Why a big blog audience didn't launch WP Engine: reputation's real payoff was recruiting
summary: Jason Cohen launched WP Engine to 18,000 blog subscribers and got just two signups, far below his 10-50 estimate. The audience's real value was recruiting a cofounder-caliber team member, and the first 50 paying customers came from other work. Fame helps, but startups stay hard.

principles.text: A large audience converts far worse than you expect; don't count on it to launch a product.
principles.quote: WPEngine got two new signups. Only two. That with 18,000 wonderful, loyal, friendly, supportive RSS subscribers and as many page-hits from Twitter and HackerNews.

principles.text: Forecasts of audience conversion can be off by an order of magnitude, so don't plan around them.
principles.quote: I figured on 10-20 new customers at minimum and dreamed of 50. I was wrong by an order of magnitude.

principles.text: Early customers come mostly from direct customer-getting work, not from the audience's halo.
principles.quote: So whatever we did without the advantage of this blog was far more important, at least for getting initial customers.

principles.text: An audience's best use may be attracting talent: your writing shows people your attitude and credentials.
principles.quote: Well we got Aaron, and it's because of this blog.

principles.text: In a commodity market you need severe differentiation or moats; a standout team can be one.
principles.quote: In a mature market you need severe points of differentiation or moats, and one of those (I felt) had to be the team itself.

principles.text: Fame is a real unfair advantage, but it doesn't make a startup easy or likely to succeed.
principles.quote: So fame does help in important ways--enough even to deserve the title of "unfair advantage"--but startups are still hard and unlikely to succeed no matter who's at the helm.
